transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Marcus (Oxford CISO), Priya (Cloud Architect), Daniel (Security Eng)
---
Summary: Quick intro + architecture deep dive focused on Private VPC.
Topics: VPC isolation, subnet mapping, ingress/egress firewalling, NAT, private endpoints, peering, KMS/HSM, SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO, audit logging retention and S3 logging, IDS/IPS, compliance requirements.
---
00:00 Marcus: alright, thanks everyone for joining, we've got about 50 minutes, we'll, uh, jump in. Marcus here, CISO at Oxford Trust. Our goal today is to understand your Private VPC architecture and what controls we can expect.
00:14 Aisha: great, thanks Marcus, I'll hand off to Liam who'll walk the architecture and then we'll dig into networking and keys and logs.
00:22 Liam: hey team, Liam O'Sullivan, Redwood SE. Quick agenda: top-level architecture, network isolation, ingress/egress controls, KMS and key management, audit logs, and then Q&A.
00:35 Priya: quick note, we run primarily in AWS us-east-1 and have tight egress policies, we want to make sure no outbound calls are opened to the public internet unless via approved proxies.
00:48 Liam: understood. At a high level for Redwood Private we deploy a customer-dedicated control plane in our managed service or optionally offer a customer-managed control plane; compute nodes run in your VPC under customer tenancy — sorry, run in your VPC — so networking and CIDRs are fully in your control.
01:10 Daniel: can you clarify, the compute runs in our account or you're spinning up instances in your account within our VPC?
01:18 Liam: good question — for the typical private VPC deployment we run the compute as customer-owned resources: either cross-account roles allow Redwood to provision, or we provide Terraform you run which creates the instances in your account. That avoids egress over public internet, everything is in your VPC.
01:36 Marcus: so that means the control plane — is it reachable from Redwood or do we host it?
01:42 Aisha: we offer both: hosted control plane (managed by Redwood and connected via private link) or a private control plane you host in your environment. For high-security customers you can self-host the control plane; we also support AWS PrivateLink to avoid internet egress for control traffic.
01:58 Priya: good, we prefer self-hosted control plane inside our VPC or at least PrivateLink. Network policy requires no public IP on compute nodes.
02:08 Liam: that's supported. Typical network layout: separate subnets for control/control-plane, inference-servers, and management. Inference nodes live in private subnets with no Internet gateway. Outbound traffic is via NAT or egress proxy that you control.
02:25 Daniel: what about model downloads/updates? Those need to pull from model repo. How is that done without public egress?
02:32 Liam: two options: pre-stage model artifacts in a customer S3 bucket or use VPC endpoints to the Redwood artifact repository via PrivateLink. For high-control customers we recommend pre-staging in S3 and restricting access to signed URLs from the infra role.
02:50 Marcus: and what about telemetry and logs that Redwood wants to collect for Console?
02:56 Aisha: logs and telemetry can be pushed to your logging infra — CloudWatch or Splunk — via VPC endpoints. We can also send aggregated metrics to Redwood Console over PrivateLink if you permit it; otherwise all observability data stays in your account.
03:15 Priya: we need to make sure audit logs are immutable and retained for 7 years. How do you handle audit logs?
03:22 Liam: the runtime can write audit logs locally and forward to a customer-provided S3 bucket via a VPC endpoint. We recommend object lock enabled on that bucket for WORM retention and cross-account logging roles.
03:40 Daniel: encryption at rest? keys?
03:43 Liam: support for AWS KMS customer-managed keys (CMK). We can also integrate with external HSM via PKCS#11 for bring-your-own-key (BYOK) in certain setups. For particularly sensitive setups we enable envelope encryption where the model weights are encrypted and keys never leave your control.
04:05 Marcus: ok that's promising. Does Redwood keep any copies outside our account?
04:09 Aisha: no, for Private VPC setups the model artifacts and inference data live in your VPC/account unless you specifically allow Redwood to access them. We can agree on data residency and policy in the contract.
04:20 Priya: ingress/egress firewalling — we have strict egress allowlist. Which outbound endpoints does Redwood need for health checks/updates?
04:29 Liam: minimal set: if you use PrivateLink endpoints, control channel is via that; otherwise outbound for OS updates and image pulls if you let us manage the hosts. If you manage hosts, host updates go through your patch pipeline. If you prefer blocked egress, we can do air-gapped image installation via signed artifacts. We'll share full endpoint list in the architecture doc.
04:54 Daniel: any IDS/IPS or network monitoring built in?
04:58 Liam: we recommend you deploy your own IDS/IPS in the VPC. Redwood provides flow logs and application-level logs; our agents can emit telemetry to a local collector that your security stack ingests. We don't ship an inline WAF by default on the data plane.
05:15 Marcus: SSO & RBAC — we use Okta. How do you integrate user auth and admin roles?
05:22 Aisha: Redwood Console supports SAML SSO (Okta, Azure AD) and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC maps to IAM roles and console groups; audit logs surface admin actions, API keys, and token usage.
05:38 Priya: token management — we want short-lived credentials and strong session policies.
05:42 Liam: we support short-lived tokens via STS and recommend ephemeral keys for operators. Service-to-service credentials use instance profiles and role assumption.
05:54 Daniel: what about model caching and KV cache — does that store any sensitive customer PII in memory or logs?
06:01 Liam: the KV cache is in-memory on the inference node and not persisted by default; if you enable persistent caching we'll encrypt at rest and you manage the keys. Logs never contain full input by default — we can redact PII in logs as part of the pipeline.
06:18 Marcus: okay, can we talk firewall specifics — e.g., do you require security groups with specific ports open?
06:23 Liam: inference nodes listen on internal ports for gRPC/HTTP from the router; we recommend using security groups that allow only the router subnets to talk to the inference nodes. Management plane access should be restricted to jump hosts or bastion subnets with MFA.
06:40 Priya: port lists please — we run very tight policies.
06:43 Liam: sure, we'll include a full port and protocol matrix in the doc. Typical ports: 443 for control plane via PrivateLink, 8022/22 disabled unless you need SSH (we prefer SSM session manager), 50051 for internal gRPC between router and worker, and ephemeral ports for KV, but again we can close everything except router subnets.
07:05 Daniel: we'd rather not open SSH at all. SSM or no access is preferred.
07:08 Liam: agreed — we support SSM Session Manager and agentless management where necessary.
07:14 Marcus: any compliance attestations you can share now? SOC 2, ISO?
07:18 Aisha: yes, we'll share SOC 2 Type II and ISO27001 certificates and the security whitepaper after the call. We'll redact client-specific info in reports.
07:28 Priya: retention policies and log shipping — we need proof of chain of custody for logs.
07:33 Liam: chain of custody can be enforced via cross-account S3 writes with CloudTrail and object lock. We can also provide signed log bundles for audits.
07:44 Daniel: TLS between components — mutual TLS?
07:46 Liam: we use mTLS for service-to-service inside the cluster and TLS for external control plane traffic; certs are rotated regularly and can be integrated with your PKI if needed.
07:58 Marcus: what about network-level segmentation — do you support multiple VPCs for dev/prod with transit gateway or VPC peering?
08:05 Liam: both are supported. Many customers use Transit Gateway or VPC peering for cross-account communication. We recommend isolating prod in its own account and peering via transit gateway with strict route tables.
08:18 Priya: if we use transit gateway, any special considerations on bandwidth or NAT translation?
08:23 Liam: throughput considerations depend on instance types; NAT is typically used for controlled outbound. We'll provide recommended instance types and baseline bandwidth numbers in the doc.
08:36 Daniel: have you done penetration tests on the Private VPC setup?
08:40 Aisha: we run internal pen tests and you can run customer-directed pen tests in the pilot — we'll agree a scope. We also run regular vulnerability scanning and produce reports.
08:53 Marcus: what about data residency — everything must stay in our region.
08:56 Liam: absolutely — we deploy regionally and can pin resources to the requested region. No cross-region replication without explicit permission.
09:06 Priya: also need to ensure backups are encrypted and in-region.
09:09 Liam: backups go to your S3 in-region and are encrypted with your CMK by default.
09:15 Daniel: KMS logs and key rotation?
09:18 Liam: key rotation is supported and you control rotation policies for CMKs. We can integrate with centralized KMS auditing for key usage logs.
09:28 Marcus: do you support external HSM vendors? We have an HSM for critical keys.
09:31 Liam: yes, we have integrations for BYOK using PKCS#11 and some HSM partners; we'll include partner list in the artifacts.
09:40 Priya: network egress to software repos was a concern — we want to vet the signatures for images.
09:44 Liam: images are signed and we can provide SBOMs; for high security we support offline image installation and signed artifacts.
09:52 Daniel: any special certificate pinning or supply chain controls?
09:55 Liam: we have supply chain controls; we'll share SBOM and the build chain details in the security packet.
10:04 Marcus: circling back to IAM — how do we ensure separation of duties?
10:08 Aisha: RBAC roles map to console roles; admin vs operator vs auditor roles. We support fine-grained permissions and you can enforce SSO with conditional access in Okta.
10:22 Priya: audit trail for admin actions — is that immutable and exportable?
10:25 Liam: yes, admin actions are logged and can be exported to your S3; logs include user, action, timestamp and resource. We also support pushing to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose.
10:40 Daniel: latency considerations — if everything is in our VPC will that affect model performance?
10:44 Liam: colocating compute in your VPC actually reduces latency to your apps. Our runtime has been validated across several instance families; we can run benchmarks during the pilot.
10:56 Marcus: ok good. Any blockers for us to start a pilot?
10:59 Aisha: none from our side; next steps are sharing artifacts, getting CIDR ranges, and scheduling the pilot kickoff — we'll make a shopping list.
11:10 Priya: timeline — we need internal approvals and procurement; aiming for pilot within 3 weeks.
11:15 Aisha: sounds doable. We'll target pilot start week of 2026-03-23.
11:22 (brief cross talk)
11:30 Liam: we'll send the architecture diagram, port matrix, endpoints, and Terraform sample. Also include the security whitepaper and SOC2/ISO artifacts.
11:40 Marcus: great — we'll review and come back with CIDR ranges and a list of outbound endpoints we allow.
11:48 Aisha: recap of action items — Aisha will send SOC2/ISO and whitepaper, Liam will send arch/terraform, Daniel to share CIDRs, Marcus to approve pilot stakeholders.
11:59 Priya: one more on retention — do you support customer-defined retention per log type?
12:03 Liam: yes, retention is configurable per log stream; we recommend aligning with regulatory retention windows.
12:12 Marcus: thanks everyone, appreciate the detail.
12:16 Aisha: thank you — we'll follow up with docs and a proposed pilot SOW.
12:22 Meeting end.
